Family Health

Pilar cysts on the scalp: diagnosis and treatment choices

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A smooth lump noticed while brushing your hair may be a pilar cyst, also called a trichilemmal cyst. These cysts commonly occur on the scalp. They are usually harmless, but an examination is important before deciding that an unfamiliar lump is one.

What makes a pilar cyst different

A pilar cyst forms from cells associated with the outer root sheath of a hair follicle. Its contents are keratin rather than ordinary oil or pus.

It usually sits under the skin as a firm, smooth, movable lump. There may be one or several, and the overlying skin often looks normal.

Unlike many epidermoid cysts, a pilar cyst usually has no visible central pore. This is a useful clinical clue, not a reliable home diagnostic test.

A quiet cyst may be painless, while pressure from a comb, headrest or tight headwear can make it uncomfortable.

Most occur on the scalp, although pilar cysts can occur elsewhere. They tend to grow slowly and range from a small pea-like bump to a much larger nodule. A new lump on the face or neck may instead be an epidermoid cyst or another condition.

They can run in families

Some people have a family tendency to develop pilar cysts. They are particularly common in middle-aged women, though age or sex alone cannot establish or exclude the diagnosis.

The cyst is not a sign that your scalp is dirty, and extra scrubbing will not remove its lining. It is not something another person catches through ordinary contact.

If relatives have similar lumps, mention this at the appointment. A family history can help explain the pattern without making every new lump automatically benign.

Most typical cysts are assessed by examination

A clinician asks about growth, pain, drainage and previous cysts and examines the lump and surrounding scalp. A typical appearance may be enough for a working diagnosis.

A biopsy or examination of a removed cyst may be recommended if there is doubt or an unusual feature. CT scans are not routine tests for an ordinary superficial pilar cyst.

If imaging is needed, the choice depends on the location, depth and diagnostic concern. You do not need a scan simply to search for hidden layers of cysts.

Inflammation does not always mean infection

A cyst can become painful and swollen after irritation or rupture. Keratin released into surrounding tissue can cause inflammation without bacteria being the main problem.

Antibiotics are useful when there is a bacterial infection, not automatically for every red or tender cyst. A clinician may recommend a different treatment for inflammation.

Seek prompt advice for rapidly worsening pain, spreading swelling or redness, pus, fever or feeling unwell. Redness may be less easy to see on darker skin.

Do not puncture, squeeze or try to cut out the lump. Even a familiar cyst can be made more difficult to treat by repeated manipulation.

Decide whether removal would help

A confirmed cyst that causes little trouble can often be watched. Removal may be reasonable if it repeatedly catches during hair care, hurts, becomes inflamed or causes substantial concern.

Surgical removal usually aims to take out the cyst and its wall under local anaesthetic. Removing only the contents leaves a greater chance that it will refill.

Ask about the incision, scar, wound care and timing of hair washing. Bleeding, infection and local changes in hair growth are possible considerations when planning scalp surgery.

Removing one cyst does not prevent new ones forming elsewhere. A later lump may be a new cyst rather than recurrence at the original site.

A changing lump deserves a fresh assessment

Rapid growth, ulceration, bleeding or a change in a longstanding lump should be assessed. Do not wait until it is painful.

Rare proliferating pilar tumors are different from an ordinary uncomplicated cyst. Some are benign and some are malignant; tissue examination is needed to classify an unusual lesion.

This does not mean typical pilar cysts commonly become cancer. The practical message is to review a changing lesion rather than predict its nature from appearance.

After removal, check how and when the result will be communicated and which wound changes should prompt a call.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Dermatology guidance describes a usually benign, keratin-filled follicular cyst that can often be diagnosed clinically and observed if comfortable.

Rupture may cause sterile inflammation rather than bacterial infection; rapid change, ulceration or an unusual lesion calls for reassessment and sometimes tissue examination.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help you record changes and prepare questions about observation, removal and wound care. A new lump needs a clinical assessment before reassurance.

When to seek help

Seek prompt care for spreading inflammation, fever, pus or worsening pain. Arrange reassessment of rapid growth, bleeding or ulceration, even without pain.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Typical pilar cysts are usually benign and often arise on the scalp.
  • Biopsy and imaging are selective, not mandatory for every lump.
  • Rapid change or increasing symptoms needs reassessment.

Frequently asked questions

Does every pilar cyst need a CT scan?

No. Typical superficial cysts are usually assessed clinically; further tests are chosen for a specific concern.

Will removal stop all future scalp cysts?

No. It treats that cyst, but new cysts may still form, especially with a family tendency.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
